# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and anatomical basis

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of cardioembolic stroke, with vast sociomedical consequences worldwide [1]. The mechanistic foundation for left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) lies in the observation that the appendage is the dominant source of thrombus in nonvalvular AF. In a landmark surgical series, Blackshear and Odell identified the left atrial appendage as the source of up to 90% of left atrial thrombi in nonvalvular AF and 57% in valvular AF [2]. The appendage is a finger-like structure whose contractility is impaired during AF, predisposing to blood stasis and thrombus formation [3]. Systemic anticoagulant drug therapy is highly effective but difficult for many patients to sustain over time, which has led to an intensive quest for alternative strategies, especially for patients at highest risk [1]. This led to the development of percutaneous devices designed to mechanically exclude the appendage from the circulation.

## Pivotal randomized evidence against warfarin

The PROTECT AF trial provided the first randomized validation of the strategy. This multicenter trial enrolled 707 patients with nonvalvular AF and CHADS2 score ≥1 to compare percutaneous closure with the Watchman device versus warfarin [4]. The composite primary efficacy end point of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death occurred at rates of 3.0% and 4.3% per 100 patient-years in the Watchman and warfarin groups, respectively, meeting noninferiority criteria [4]. However, early safety was a concern: there was a significantly higher risk of complications, predominantly pericardial effusion and procedural stroke related to air embolism [5]. Importantly, there is a significant improvement in safety with operator experience [5].

The confirmatory PREVAIL trial enrolled higher-risk patients and mandated new operators [6]. At 18 months the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve prespecified noninferiority, while early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF [6]. The failure to meet one endpoint was attributed largely to an unexpectedly low event rate in the warfarin control arm [6]. The 5-year patient-level meta-analysis of both trials clarified the long-term picture: LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke, and mortality [7]. A pooled analysis confirmed a favorable net clinical benefit relative to warfarin [8].

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation

Because the pivotal trials enrolled anticoagulation-eligible patients, the ASAP study addressed those who were not. This multicenter, prospective study examined LAAC with the Watchman device in 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and CHADS2 score ≥1 who were considered ineligible for warfarin [9]. Serious procedure- or device-related safety events occurred in 8.7% of patients, and outcomes supported feasibility of a device-plus-antiplatelet strategy without a warfarin transition [9].

## Newer devices and head-to-head comparisons

Device iteration has improved closure and safety. In the single-arm PINNACLE FLX trial of the next-generation Watchman FLX, the primary safety endpoint event rate was 0.5% and the primary effectiveness endpoint of effective closure at 1 year was 100% [10]. The Amulet IDE trial provided the first large head-to-head randomized comparison of two devices: the Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [11]. The SWISS-APERO trial similarly compared the two devices in routine practice [12].

## Comparison with direct oral anticoagulants

As DOACs supplanted warfarin, the PRAGUE-17 trial directly compared LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients. It randomized patients with nonvalvular AF and a history of cardioembolism, clinically-relevant bleeding, or both CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HAS-BLED ≥2 to LAAC or DOACs (95% apixaban) [13]. In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for major events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [13]. More recently, the OPTION trial randomized 1600 AF patients undergoing catheter ablation to LAAC or oral anticoagulation [14]. LAAO was noninferior to OAC for the composite primary endpoint of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and was superior to OAC for non–procedure-related bleeding [14].

## Device-related thrombus and real-world safety

Device-related thrombus (DRT) remains an important complication. A multicenter registry found that DRT presence was associated with a higher risk of the composite endpoint of death, ischemic stroke, or systemic embolization, driven by ischemic stroke [15], and identified predictors including hypercoagulability, renal insufficiency, deep implantation, and non-paroxysmal AF. A pooled meta-analysis reinforced that stroke incidence was 11.5% in DRT patients versus 2.9% among non-DRT patients [16]. Real-world experience has been reassuring: in the NCDR LAAO Registry, in-hospital major adverse events occurred in 2.1% of patients—including pericardial effusion in 1.4% and major bleeding in 1.2%—with rates more favorable than in the two randomized Watchman trials [17].

## Surgical context and guidelines

The role of appendage exclusion extends to cardiac surgery. In LAAOS III, among patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery, most of whom continued antithrombotic therapy, the risk of stroke or systemic embolism was lower with concomitant surgical occlusion [18], demonstrating additive benefit on top of anticoagulation. Current guidelines reflect this evolving evidence: the 2024 ESC/EACTS guidelines retain the indication for percutaneous LAAO in patients with contraindications to oral anticoagulation (class IIb) [19], while noting persistent uncertainty about optimal post-implant antithrombotic therapy [20].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has matured from concept to a guideline-supported therapy, with randomized data establishing noninferiority to warfarin and DOACs and reductions in hemorrhagic events. Ongoing priorities include refining patient selection, minimizing device-related thrombus and peri-device leak, and defining optimal antithrombotic regimens.
